video_title: The Inference Frontier: from 100 to 10,000 tokens per second — Sean Lie, Cerebras CTO
gist: Recorded the day after Hot Chips 2026, Cerebras CTO Sean Lie details CS4's new modular Nexus platform, previews a CS5 chip hitting up to 10,000 tokens/sec, and unpacks the OpenAI-Cerebras 'ultra fast' partnership alongside pointed takes on why Groq's new chip and Etched's $20B valuation don't hold up under scrutiny.

insights.claim: Cerebras's CS4 system is built on a new modular 'Nexus' platform that delivers twice the power to the wafer, twice the interconnect bandwidth, and half the latency of the prior generation, with the gains engineered entirely at the system architecture level (not just the chip); the same modular platform was designed from the ground up to support multiple future chip generations, including next year's CS5 wafer.
insights.speaker: Sean Lie
insights.so_what: System-level (power/interconnect/packaging) redesign, not just chip shrink, is now Cerebras's main performance lever, and the modular platform lets it amortize that investment across multiple product generations — relevant to how fast/cheaply Cerebras can iterate versus rivals doing full redesigns each cycle.
insights.quote: twice the amount of power to the wafer than we have in our previous generation. Um twice the amount of uh interconnect bandwidth, half the latency.

insights.claim: At Hot Chips, Cerebras demoed the GPT-OSS model running on CS4 at over 4,400 tokens per second, which the company uses to back its claim of being roughly 30x faster than GPUs.
insights.speaker: Sean Lie
insights.so_what: A concrete, named benchmark investors can use to sanity-check Cerebras's 'ultra-fast inference' marketing claims against Nvidia GPU baselines and rival chip vendors.
insights.quote: we're showing uh GPTOSS uh running at over 4,400 TPS which is just mind-blowing.

insights.claim: Cerebras previewed its next wafer-scale chip (CS5, arriving next year on the same Nexus platform) delivering roughly another 2x performance jump: medium-sized models like GPT-OSS and Gemma running up to 10,000 tokens/second, and frontier-scale models like Kimi and DeepSeek running up to 5,000 tokens/second.
insights.speaker: Sean Lie
insights.so_what: Sets a concrete, dated (next-year) throughput target the market can hold Cerebras to, and reframes 'ultra-fast inference' benchmarks upward for the whole industry.
insights.quote: you'll be able to run, you know, medium-sized models like GPOSS or Gemma at speeds up to 10,000 TPS and even frontier level models like Kimmy or DeepSeek ... up to 5,000 TPS.

insights.claim: Lie frames Cerebras's first generations of wafer-scale chips as a pure 'technology demonstration' phase meant to prove the architecture was buildable at all (when skeptics told the company it was 'insane'), and says the company has now shifted into a scaling phase focused on capacity, reliability, and keeping a hardware flywheel going now that demand (via OpenAI) has validated the bet.
insights.speaker: Sean Lie
insights.so_what: Marks an inflection from R&D/technology risk to execution/scaling risk in Cerebras's story — the relevant investor question shifts from 'can they build it' to 'can they scale and supply it fast enough.'

insights.claim: Cerebras says it is currently sold out of all the inference capacity it is building, and is strategically allocating every megawatt, with a large share going to OpenAI as its biggest partner — a relationship the company frames as commercial plus genuine model/hardware co-design.
insights.speaker: Sean Lie
insights.so_what: Sold-out capacity signals real scarcity-driven demand for ultra-fast inference rather than a speculative build-out, relevant to how investors read Cerebras's post-IPO growth runway.
insights.quote: right now uh we are basically you know sold out of everything that we're building right.

insights.claim: Through the OpenAI-Cerebras 'ultra fast' inference launch, OpenAI's largest, most capable ('frontier') model runs about 14x faster than on OpenAI's normal GPU-based inference stack.
insights.speaker: Sean Lie
insights.so_what: A concrete speed multiple that anchors the pricing/positioning of Cerebras-powered 'ultra fast' tiers versus standard GPU inference.
insights.quote: we're running uh uh you know frontier level one of the most intelligent models right open's largest, most capable, most intelligent model right now at 14 times faster than their normal, you know, GPU speeds.

insights.claim: OpenAI is reportedly using much of its Cerebras allocation internally first, before opening it to enterprise customers — specifically for incident-response teams (where every second/minute during an outage matters) and for critical research applications where extra reasoning throughput drives more intelligent responses.
insights.speaker: Sean Lie
insights.so_what: Reveals an under-the-radar operational use case for ultra-fast inference (internal ops/incident response, research iteration speed) beyond chatbot latency — a demand driver investors may be underweighting.
insights.quote: they're using it in like their incident response uh teams, right? When there's an outage in their service, for example, every single second, every single minute matters.

insights.claim: Lie agrees with the host's observation that OpenAI didn't have to expose ultra-fast Cerebras-powered inference to enterprise customers at all — it could have kept the capacity fully internal — and reads OpenAI's decision to sell it externally as a deliberate balancing of its stated mission against its need to operate as a business, especially with IPO speculation in the background.
insights.speaker: Sean Lie
insights.so_what: A read on OpenAI's monetization and IPO-prep strategy from a close infrastructure partner's vantage point — worth tracking as a signal of OpenAI's near-term commercial priorities.
insights.quote: there's, you know, talks about them going IPO and all this and so very much even externally, you can see they're balancing both of these.

insights.claim: Lie confirms Cerebras's recent IPO was the largest semiconductor IPO in history, while noting the company still feels it is early in its growth trajectory.
insights.speaker: Sean Lie
insights.so_what: A public-market anchor point for Cerebras's scale and investor attention heading into the CS4/CS5 ramp.
insights.quote: it was like the largest like you know semiconductor IPO in history.

themes.theme: Jalapeno and Groq: competing chip bets

insights.claim: Lie says the most exciting thing about OpenAI's Jalapeno chip (revealed at Hot Chips) isn't its raw performance numbers but the fact that it was built using an 'AI-first' design methodology that let OpenAI build the chip faster — and he expects AI-driven chip design to become standard across the semiconductor industry.
insights.speaker: Sean Lie
insights.so_what: Points to AI-assisted chip design (EDA/design-methodology disruption) as an industry-wide shift worth tracking, not just a one-off OpenAI project — relevant to EDA vendors and AI-for-chip-design startups.
insights.quote: Having an AI first methodology enabled them to, you know, build the chip faster and achieve some of these very impressive results, right? And that is 100% the future of our industry.

insights.claim: Jalapeno was specialized for throughput rather than latency, while Cerebras is pushing the latency/ultra-fast end (up to 10,000 TPS with CS5); OpenAI and Cerebras plan to combine both chip types once Jalapeno and CS5 are available next year into a 'full fast inference portfolio,' potentially including prefill/decode disaggregation across the two architectures.
insights.speaker: Sean Lie
insights.so_what: Suggests OpenAI's future inference stack will be heterogeneous (its own throughput chip plus Cerebras's latency chip) rather than single-vendor — a template other labs may copy, and a moat for Cerebras via deepening co-design lock-in.

insights.claim: Lie argues it is telling that Groq's new chip (unveiled at Hot Chips) was only benchmarked on a small, non-disaggregated ~30-31 billion parameter model, which he interprets as evidence that Groq's non-wafer-scale SRAM architecture doesn't have enough on-chip memory to run frontier-scale models efficiently — estimating it would take 'thousands and thousands' of Groq LPUs just to hold the weights of a multi-trillion-parameter frontier model.
insights.speaker: Sean Lie
insights.so_what: A specific, falsifiable competitive thesis against Groq: watch whether Groq ever publishes disaggregated or frontier-scale-model benchmarks; continued absence would corroborate the memory-wall critique.
insights.quote: you need thousands and thousands of Grock LPUs just to hold the the weights.

insights.claim: Lie predicts Groq will end up focusing on significantly smaller models rather than frontier-scale ones because of this architectural memory limitation, contrasting it with Cerebras's wafer, which he says has roughly two orders of magnitude (about 100x) more memory per chip than a single Groq chip.
insights.speaker: Sean Lie
insights.so_what: A testable market-segmentation call: if it plays out, Groq and Cerebras end up serving different tiers of the inference market (small/cheap models vs. frontier-scale) rather than competing head-on.
insights.quote: I think what's what's going to end up happening is they're going to end up focusing on significantly smaller models.

insights.claim: Lie flags it as suspicious that Nvidia's Rubin CPX product — despite Jensen Huang spending significant GTC stage time explaining attention/FFN disaggregation — launched in full production showing performance numbers only on a non-disaggregated, small (~31B parameter) model.
insights.speaker: Sean Lie
insights.so_what: Raises doubt about whether Nvidia's much-hyped attention/FFN disaggregation story is actually production-ready — worth checking Nvidia's next disclosed benchmarks against this claim.
insights.quote: it it it's very suspicious that they're um that their product that's in full production, they've only shown performance numbers on a non-disaggregated 31 billion parameter model.

insights.claim: Lie characterizes Nvidia, AMD, Trainium, and TPU as all fundamentally pursuing the same strategy of 'building a better Rubin' — i.e., a faster general-purpose accelerator — which he calls valuable but distinct from Cerebras's bet on an entirely different vector: ultra-low-latency, single-stream inference speed.
insights.speaker: Sean Lie
insights.so_what: A clear positioning framework for evaluating AI accelerator vendors: incumbents compete on throughput/cost-per-token improvements on a common GPU-like paradigm, while Cerebras is deliberately not on that treadmill.
insights.quote: AMD, Tranium, in many ways TPU, like all of these in my mind are all trying to build a better Reuben.

insights.claim: Lie predicts inference infrastructure is moving toward a heterogeneous, disaggregated ecosystem where different specialized hardware handles different sub-tasks within a single inference request — not just prefill/decode split, but finer breakdowns like KV-cache loading, attention computation, and expert routing/balancing across mixture-of-experts models — which only becomes economical at hundred-megawatt-to-gigawatt data center scale.
insights.speaker: Sean Lie
insights.so_what: Implies future AI data centers will look like heterogeneous compute fabrics rather than homogeneous GPU pods once scale crosses a gigawatt threshold — a structural thesis relevant to interconnect and systems-integration investment.
insights.quote: at that point, it's as if you're like thinking about the entire data center as if it's like one computer.

insights.claim: Lie argues what used to count as 'fast' inference (100-200 tokens/second) is quickly becoming the new 'batch mode' — still valuable for prompt processing and highly parallel offline workloads (e.g., running evals overnight in two hours instead of twenty), but no longer sufficient on its own, since agentic workflows require many sequential reasoning loops that demand much higher per-stream speed to be practical.
insights.speaker: Sean Lie
insights.so_what: Reframes the industry's 'fast inference' bar upward — investors evaluating any inference product's speed claims should benchmark against thousands of tokens/second, not hundreds, especially for agentic use cases.
insights.quote: what used to be considered fast at like 1,000 uh 100 or or 200 tokens per second is quickly becoming the new batch mode.

themes.theme: Packaging and memory as the next chip frontier

insights.claim: Lie says the biggest lesson from building wafer-scale chips was that the hardest problems weren't inter-die interconnect or yield (though those were real, fundamental challenges) but power delivery, cooling, and reliability at scale — and he predicts emerging 3D-DRAM-stacking efforts from companies like Dmatrix and Samsung will hit the same real-world engineering wall once they move past conceptual diagrams.
insights.speaker: Sean Lie
insights.so_what: A due-diligence heuristic for any next-gen chip-packaging startup: ask specifically about power delivery, cooling, and reliability at scale, not just the elegance of the packaging concept.
insights.quote: it's, you know, one thing to draw, you know, a PowerPoint slide with a DRAM and and uh and logic and then it's another to actually make it work.

insights.claim: Cerebras has run its own DRAM-stacking program for two years (announced at this Hot Chips), aiming to bring 3D memory integration into future products in a way Lie analogizes to the wafer's existing 3D power-delivery 'backpack' — positioning Cerebras alongside Dmatrix and Samsung in the memory-integration race, not just as a compute/wafer company.
insights.speaker: Sean Lie
insights.so_what: Signals a second, less-publicized R&D track at Cerebras (memory packaging IP) that could feed future generations or become a differentiated technology asset beyond wafer-scale compute alone.
insights.quote: we also started two years ago our um DRAM stacking program for the very same same reason.

insights.claim: Lie expresses open skepticism of Etched, a chip startup now valued around $20 billion: he notes it has published no public benchmark numbers, has changed its stated technical approach over time, makes claims (e.g., 'distributed storage' that is somehow faster because it's distributed) he says he doesn't understand, and — based on what's public, including a rack shown at Hot Chips — doesn't appear to be building anything beyond an incrementally better GPU.
insights.speaker: Sean Lie
insights.so_what: A specific, named bear case on a richly-valued AI chip startup from a credible industry insider — worth stress-testing Etched's claims against real benchmarks before they become public.
insights.quote: no numbers, no benchmarks... it's very impressive graphics design but I also don't see them building anything beyond just or trying to build something better than just you know a traditional GPU.

insights.claim: Lie says the next major lever in AI compute performance is integration 'outside the chip' — the rack, node, package, interconnect, and even the manufacturing/fab process itself — because models and applications are now too large for any single chip to matter in isolation; he also frames AI chip design as reducible to three fundamentals (compute, interconnect, memory), with memory bandwidth specifically being the key bottleneck for low-latency inference.
insights.speaker: Sean Lie
insights.so_what: Points investors toward systems/packaging/interconnect and memory-bandwidth innovation — not raw compute FLOPS — as the more durable differentiator in the next phase of AI hardware competition.
insights.quote: everything comes down to the integration. Everything comes down to how do you bring together more compute? How do you bring together more memory? How do you bring together more interconnect, right?

insights.claim: Lie says the single biggest untapped opportunity for Cerebras and the entire non-Nvidia hardware ecosystem is that nearly all current models are architected and tuned for specific Nvidia GPUs (e.g., B200, GB200, NVL72) — and that even small adjustments to a model's architecture for alternative hardware could unlock 'massive gains' on top of the already-demonstrated 14x speedup achieved with an unmodified, Nvidia-optimized model.
insights.speaker: Sean Lie
insights.so_what: A concrete alpha thesis: watch for labs that begin architecting models explicitly for non-Nvidia inference hardware (starting with OpenAI's Jalapeno/Cerebras co-design) — that's where the next step-change in inference efficiency is likely to come from, not further scaling on the current GPU-tuned model designs.
insights.quote: if you start to then open up the possibility of adjusting that model architecture even slightly, you can get massive gains.

insights.claim: Both host and Lie flag AI-generated/AI-assisted chip kernel code as an underrated trend that specifically benefits companies like Cerebras.
insights.speaker: Sean Lie
insights.so_what: AI coding agents applied to low-level kernel writing could help non-Nvidia hardware vendors close their software/ecosystem gap with CUDA faster than expected — a trend worth tracking alongside model-hardware co-design.
insights.quote: the people under are really sleeping on AI codegen for kernels.

insights.claim: Lie states the open-source AI model market is now roughly 95% dominated by Chinese labs — most of the high-quality, openly available large models come from China — which he calls a strategically challenging dependency for the broader ecosystem even as the openness itself benefits the global community.
insights.speaker: Sean Lie
insights.so_what: Quantifies a concentration risk at the open-weights layer of the AI stack that matters to any US company building products on open-source models, and to policymakers weighing export controls and domestic model investment.
insights.quote: the open- source model market is 100% Chinese right um not 100% but almost okay 95% right.

insights.claim: Lie notes that hardware and infrastructure to support Chinese AI models is being built up in parallel and independently of US supply chains, and argues that sustaining US competitiveness against this can't be solved by any single company or fab — it requires a coordinated, national/government-level strategic initiative, which he says Cerebras has been pushing for and supporting.
insights.speaker: Sean Lie
insights.so_what: Reinforces the policy-driven investment case around US semiconductor subsidies, export controls, and domestic AI-infra buildout as themes that industry insiders view as urgent and unresolved.
insights.quote: it's needs government level natural national interest level kind of initiative to be able to make this happen.
